title: Count Divisible Seat Orders
statement:
Seats are numbered 1 to n, and so are n guests. Every guest sits in exactly one seat. A seating is good if, for every seat i holding guest g, either g is divisible by i or i is divisible by g.

Return how many good seatings exist.

examples.why: The good orders are 1 2 3, 2 1 3 and 3 2 1. Guest 3 cannot sit in seat 2 and guest 2 cannot sit in seat 3, which rules out the other three.
Guest 3 must sit in seat 1 or 3, which prunes most of the 24 orders.
One guest, one seat, and 1 divides 1.

hints: Fill the seats one at a time. At each seat, which guests are still allowed?
Backtrack: try every unused guest that fits the current seat, recurse, then undo. A bad prefix is dropped immediately instead of being finished.
Fill the seats from n down to 1: high seats accept very few guests, so dead ends show up early. For a faster count, memoize on the set of guests already seated (a bitmask).

explain.intuition:
There are n! seatings, about 1.3 trillion for n = 15, so listing them is out. But the divisibility rule is very restrictive: seat 13 accepts only guests 1 and 13. Backtracking places one guest at a time and abandons a partial seating the moment a seat has no valid guest, so most of the n! orders are never built.

Order matters: start with the high seats, which have the fewest options, so wrong branches die near the root. Going further, notice that once you know which guests are already seated, the seat to fill next is fixed (it is the number of seated guests plus one), so the count for the rest depends only on that set. Memoizing on a bitmask gives an O(n · 2ⁿ) solution.
steps: Keep a used marker for each guest.
Define place(seat): if seat == 0, one complete seating was found, return 1.
Otherwise, for every unused guest g with g % seat == 0 or seat % g == 0: mark it used, add place(seat − 1), then unmark it.
pitfalls: Checking only one direction of divisibility. Guest 2 in seat 4 is good because 4 is divisible by 2.
Generating all permutations first and filtering at the end. That is n! work with no pruning.
Forgetting to unmark a guest after the recursive call, so later branches think it is still taken.

complexity.time: Bounded by the number of valid partial seatings, far below n!; O(n · 2ⁿ) with the bitmask memo
complexity.space: O(n) for backtracking, O(2ⁿ) with the memo

solutions.title: Backtracking from the last seat
solutions.idea: Place guests seat by seat, starting with seat n, and skip any guest that breaks the rule.
solutions.time: Far below O(n!) thanks to pruning

solutions.title: Bitmask DP over seated guests
solutions.idea: ways[mask] counts good ways to fill seats 1..popcount(mask) with exactly the guests in mask. Add the next seat's guest from those not in mask.

followups: Return one good seating, or all of them, instead of the count.
Why does filling seats from n down to 1 run faster than from 1 up to n, even though both count the same thing?
